records.source: וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ אֲבִימֶ֤לֶךְ בֶּן־יְרֻבַּ֨עַל֙ שְׁכֶ֔מָה אֶל־אֲחֵ֖י אִמּ֑וֹ וַיְדַבֵּ֣ר אֲלֵיהֶ֔ם וְאֶל־כָּל־מִשְׁפַּ֛חַת בֵּית־אֲבִ֥י אִמּ֖וֹ לֵאמֹֽר׃
records.gloss: And went Abimelech son of Jerubbaal to Shechem, to [the] brothers of his mother, and spoke to them and to all [the] clan of [the] house of [the] father of his mother, saying,
pieces: Abimelech son of Jerubbaal went to his mother's relatives in Shechem and spoke to them and to the whole clan of his mother's family. He said,

L.1: And Abimelech son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem, to his mother's brothers, and spoke to them and to all the clan of the house of his mother's father, saying,

R.1: Abimelech was a son of Jerubbaal, the man also called Gideon. Abimelech went to Shechem, where his mother's relatives lived. He spoke to them and to everyone in his mother's family clan. He said,

decisions.choice: Abimelech son of Jerubbaal: Gideon's son by his concubine from Shechem
decisions.reason: Jerubbaal is Gideon's other name (6:32; 7:1). Gideon had seventy sons by his many wives (8:30), and Abimelech was the son of his concubine who lived in Shechem (8:31). That is why Abimelech turns to his mother's family there: through her he belongs to Shechem, while his half-brothers belong to Ophrah.

decisions.choice: his mother's brothers: his relatives on his mother's side
decisions.reason: The word "brothers" often means kinsmen in general (Genesis 13:8; 29:15). The next words widen the circle to the whole clan of his mother's father, so the men meant are her family, not only her own brothers.

decisions.choice: Abimelech: the name means "my father is king"
decisions.reason: Gideon refused to rule over Israel and said that neither he nor his son would rule; the LORD would rule (8:22-23). Yet he gave this son a name that means "my father is king" (8:31). The chapter tells how the son tried to make the name come true.

decisions.choice: relatives / his mother's family
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "relatives" and "family" for "brothers" and "house of the father", since the Hebrew means the wider kin (m2). Literal keeps "brothers".

decisions.choice: the man also called Gideon
decisions.reason: Readable reminds the reader that Jerubbaal is Gideon, the hero of chapters 6-8, which the Hebrew assumes the reader knows (6:32).

records.heading: Abimelech kills his brothers

records.source: דַּבְּרוּ־נָ֞א בְּאָזְנֵ֨י כָל־בַּעֲלֵ֣י שְׁכֶם֮ מַה־טּ֣וֹב לָכֶם֒ הַמְשֹׁ֨ל בָּכֶ֜ם שִׁבְעִ֣ים אִ֗ישׁ כֹּ֚ל בְּנֵ֣י יְרֻבַּ֔עַל אִם־מְשֹׁ֥ל בָּכֶ֖ם אִ֣ישׁ אֶחָ֑ד וּזְכַרְתֶּ֕ם כִּֽי־עַצְמֵכֶםוּבְשַׂרְכֶ֖ם אָנִֽי׃
records.gloss: Speak, please, in [the] ears of all [the] lords of Shechem: what [is] good for you, to rule over you seventy men, all [the] sons of Jerubbaal, or to rule over you one man? And remember that your bone and your flesh I [am].
pieces: "Please put this question to all the leaders of Shechem: 'Which is better for you, to be ruled by seventy men, all the sons of Jerubbaal, or to be ruled by one man? Remember that I am your own flesh and blood.'"

L.2: "Speak, please, in the ears of all the lords of Shechem: 'Which [is] better for you, that seventy men, all the sons of Jerubbaal, rule over you, or that one man rule over you? And remember that I [am] your bone and your flesh.'"

R.2: "Ask all the leaders of Shechem this: 'Would you rather have all seventy of Jerubbaal's sons ruling over you, or just one man? Remember, I am your own relative.'"

decisions.choice: the lords of Shechem: the leading landholders who governed the city
decisions.reason: The word ba'al means owner or master, and "the ba'als of a city" are its free landowning men, the body that could make decisions for the city, make a king (verse 6) and break with him (verse 23). The phrase comes back sixteen times in this chapter. It is the same word as the name of the god Baal, whose temple they serve (verse 4), so the story plays on who is truly lord in Shechem.

decisions.choice: seventy ruling, or one: a choice Gideon had refused
decisions.reason: Gideon had said that neither he nor his sons would rule over Israel (8:22-23), and nothing says his sons ruled after him. Abimelech's question takes their rule for granted, to make one ruler look like the better choice.

decisions.choice: your bone and your flesh: your blood relative
decisions.reason: "Bone and flesh" is the language of close kinship (Genesis 2:23; 29:14; 2 Samuel 5:1). Abimelech's claim is that he is one of Shechem's own, unlike his brothers from Ophrah.

decisions.choice: lords (Literal); leaders (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "lords", which shows the root "owner, master" and its link with the god Baal. Balanced and Readable say "leaders", since "lords" suggests nobles or a feudal title to a modern reader. The same rendering is used through the chapter.

decisions.choice: your own flesh and blood / your own relative
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the English idiom for kinship, Readable the plain word; Literal keeps "bone and flesh".

records.source: וַיְדַבְּר֨וּ אֲחֵֽי־אִמּ֜וֹ עָלָ֗יו בְּאָזְנֵי֙ כָּל־בַּעֲלֵ֣י שְׁכֶ֔ם אֵ֥ת כָּל־הַדְּבָרִ֖ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וַיֵּ֤ט לִבָּם֙ אַחֲרֵ֣י אֲבִימֶ֔לֶךְ כִּ֥י אָמְר֖וּ אָחִ֥ינוּ הֽוּא׃
records.gloss: And spoke [the] brothers of his mother concerning him in [the] ears of all [the] lords of Shechem all these words, and inclined their heart after Abimelech, for they said, our brother [is] he.
pieces: His mother's relatives spoke on his behalf and put all these words before the leaders of Shechem, and their hearts leaned toward Abimelech, because they said, "He is our own kin."

L.3: And his mother's brothers spoke all these words about him in the ears of all the lords of Shechem, and their heart inclined after Abimelech, for they said, "He [is] our brother."

R.3: So his mother's relatives told all the leaders of Shechem what Abimelech had said. The leaders decided to follow Abimelech, because they said, "He is one of us."

decisions.choice: their heart inclined after Abimelech: they were won over to his side
decisions.reason: The heart is where a person decides. To have one's heart "incline after" someone is to lean toward him and choose to back him (1 Kings 11:3 uses the same picture for turning away).

decisions.choice: our brother: our own kin, one of us
decisions.reason: As in verse 1, "brother" means kinsman. The lords back him because his mother's family is from Shechem (8:31), not for anything he has done.

decisions.choice: He is one of us
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of "our brother" (m2), since a young reader would take "brother" literally.

records.source: וַיִּתְּנוּ־לוֹ֙ שִׁבְעִ֣ים כֶּ֔סֶף מִבֵּ֖יתּבַ֣עַלבְּרִ֑ית וַיִּשְׂכֹּ֨ר בָּהֶ֜ם אֲבִימֶ֗לֶךְ אֲנָשִׁ֤ים רֵיקִים֙ וּפֹ֣חֲזִ֔ים וַיֵּלְכ֖וּ אַחֲרָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And they gave to him seventy [pieces of] silver from [the] house of Baal-berith, and hired with them Abimelech men empty and reckless, and they went after him.
pieces: They gave him seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal-berith, and with that money Abimelech hired worthless, reckless men, who became his followers.

L.4: And they gave him seventy [pieces of] silver from the house of Baal-berith, and with it Abimelech hired empty and reckless men, and they followed him.

R.4: They gave him seventy pieces of silver from the temple of the god Baal-berith. Abimelech used the money to pay a gang of worthless troublemakers to follow him.

decisions.choice: the house of Baal-berith: the temple of "Baal of the covenant" in Shechem
decisions.reason: After Gideon died, Israel made Baal-berith its god (8:33). The name means "Baal of the covenant"; in verse 46 the god is called El-berith, "God of the covenant". Temples kept treasuries, so the money for Abimelech's plot came from the god's own store.

decisions.choice: seventy pieces of silver: one for each brother he would kill
decisions.reason: The weight is not named, though shekels are likely, which would make it a little under two pounds of silver. The number matches the seventy sons of Jerubbaal (verse 5): the price of the plot is one piece of silver a head.

decisions.choice: empty and reckless men: worthless men with nothing to lose, ready for anything
decisions.reason: "Empty" men are men of no worth or standing, the kind who gather round an outlaw (11:3; 2 Chronicles 13:7). "Reckless" describes people who act without restraint (Zephaniah 3:4). They are hired muscle, not an army.

decisions.choice: temple
decisions.reason: "House" of a god means its temple; Balanced and Readable say so. Literal keeps "house".

decisions.choice: the god Baal-berith
decisions.reason: Readable adds "the god" so that a new reader knows Baal-berith is a god, not a person.

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֤א בֵית־אָבִיו֙ עָפְרָ֔תָה וַֽיַּהֲרֹ֞ג אֶת־אֶחָ֧יו בְּנֵֽי־יְרֻבַּ֛עַל שִׁבְּעִ֥יםאִ֖ישׁ עַל־אֶ֣בֶן אֶחָ֑ת וַיִּוָּתֵ֞ר יוֹתָ֧ם בֶּן־יְרֻבַּ֛עַל הַקָּטֹ֖ן כִּ֥י נֶחְבָּֽא׃ס
records.gloss: And he went [to the] house of his father at Ophrah, and killed his brothers, [the] sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone; and was left Jotham, son of Jerubbaal, the youngest, for he hid himself.
pieces: He went to his father's home at Ophrah and killed his brothers, the seventy sons of Jerubbaal, on a single stone. But Jotham, Jerubbaal's youngest son, survived because he had gone into hiding.

L.5: And he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, was left, for he hid himself.

R.5: He went to his father's home in the town of Ophrah. There, on one stone, he killed his brothers, the seventy sons of Jerubbaal. Only Jotham, the youngest son, was left alive, because he hid.

decisions.choice: on one stone: killed one after another in one place, like a slaughter
decisions.reason: Killing them all on one stone makes the murder a single, deliberate execution. A stone was where animals were slaughtered (1 Samuel 14:33-34), so the phrase may also make the deed look like a sacrifice. Jotham repeats the words in verse 18, and the chapter ends with a stone falling on Abimelech's head (verse 53).

decisions.choice: seventy men: the whole number of Gideon's sons, given in round figures
decisions.reason: Gideon had seventy sons (8:30), and Jotham, one of them, escapes. So either "seventy" is the round number for all of them, or Gideon's sons with Abimelech made seventy-one. Either way the point is that the whole family was wiped out but one.

decisions.choice: the town of Ophrah
decisions.reason: Readable adds "the town of" so that a new reader knows Ophrah is a place (6:11).

records.source: וַיֵּאָ֨סְפ֜וּ כָּל־בַּעֲלֵ֤י שְׁכֶם֙ וְכָל־בֵּ֣ית מִלּ֔וֹא וַיֵּ֣לְכ֔וּ וַיַּמְלִ֥יכוּ אֶת־אֲבִימֶ֖לֶךְ לְמֶ֑לֶךְ עִם־אֵל֥וֹן מֻצָּ֖ב אֲשֶׁ֥ר בִּשְׁכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And gathered all [the] lords of Shechem and all Beth-millo, and they went and made king Abimelech as king by [the] oak of [the] pillar that [is] in Shechem.
pieces: Then all the leaders of Shechem and all of Beth-millo came together and went and made Abimelech king beside the oak of the standing stone at Shechem.

L.6: And all the lords of Shechem and all Beth-millo gathered, and they went and made Abimelech king by the oak of the pillar that [is] in Shechem.

R.6: Then all the leaders of Shechem and everyone from Beth-millo met together. They made Abimelech their king beside the oak tree near the standing stone in Shechem.

decisions.choice: Beth-millo: a fortified part of Shechem, or the people who held it
decisions.reason: The name means "house of the filling", probably a fort built on a raised platform of packed earth (compare "the Millo" in Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 5:9). It may be the same place as the Tower of Shechem (verses 46-49). Its exact site is not known.

decisions.choice: the oak of the pillar at Shechem: the place where Israel had sworn to serve the LORD
decisions.reason: At Shechem Joshua set up a great stone under the oak by the sanctuary as a witness to Israel's covenant with the LORD (Joshua 24:25-27). Jacob had buried foreign gods under the oak at Shechem (Genesis 35:4). Abimelech is made king at the very spot where Israel had promised to serve God alone.

decisions.choice: the standing stone
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word means something set up, here a stone pillar (m2). Balanced and Readable say "standing stone" so that it is not taken for a building's column; Literal keeps "pillar".

records.heading: Jotham speaks from Mount Gerizim

records.source: וַיַּגִּ֣דוּ לְיוֹתָ֗ם וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ֙ וַֽיַּעֲמֹד֙ בְּרֹ֣אשׁ הַר־גְּרִזִ֔ים וַיִּשָּׂ֥א קוֹל֖וֹ וַיִּקְרָ֑א וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֗ם שִׁמְע֤וּ אֵלַי֙ בַּעֲלֵ֣י שְׁכֶ֔ם וְיִשְׁמַ֥ע אֲלֵיכֶ֖ם אֱלֹהִֽים׃
records.gloss: And they told Jotham, and he went and stood on [the] top of Mount Gerizim, and lifted his voice and called, and said to them, listen to me, lords of Shechem, and may listen to you God.
pieces: When Jotham was told about it, he went and stood on the summit of Mount Gerizim and shouted out to them, "Listen to me, leaders of Shechem, so that God will listen to you.

L.7: And they told Jotham, and he went and stood on the top of Mount Gerizim, and he lifted up his voice and called out and said to them, "Listen to me, lords of Shechem, so that God may listen to you.

R.7: When Jotham heard about it, he climbed to the top of Mount Gerizim. He shouted down to them, "Listen to me, leaders of Shechem, if you want God to listen to you!

decisions.choice: Mount Gerizim: the mountain of blessing that rises over Shechem
decisions.reason: Gerizim stands just above the city. Moses ordered that the blessings of the covenant be spoken from Gerizim and the curses from Ebal (Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:12), and Joshua did so (Joshua 8:33). From the mountain of blessing Jotham speaks what turns into a curse (verse 57).

decisions.choice: listen to me, so that God may listen to you: hearing Jotham is the condition of God's hearing them
decisions.reason: The second verb depends on the first: if the lords will listen to Jotham's case, God will listen to them. It warns them that their standing before God depends on how they answer for what was done to Jerubbaal's house.

decisions.choice: if you want God to listen to you
decisions.reason: Readable makes the link between the two clauses plain (m2).

records.source: הָל֤וֹךְ הָֽלְכוּ֙ הָעֵצִ֔ים לִמְשֹׁ֥חַ עֲלֵיהֶ֖ם מֶ֑לֶךְ וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ לַזַּ֖יִת מָלְכָ֥ה עָלֵֽינוּ׃
records.gloss: Going they went, the trees, to anoint over them a king, and they said to the olive tree, reign over us.
pieces: One day the trees set out to anoint a king to rule them. \q They went to the olive tree and said, 'Be our king.'

L.8: Once the trees went out to anoint a king over themselves, \q and they said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.'

R.8: Once upon a time the trees went out to choose one of them and anoint it as their king. \q They said to the olive tree, 'Be our king.'

decisions.choice: the trees went out: a fable, a story in which plants speak
decisions.reason: Jotham tells a fable, a short tale with talking plants that teaches a lesson, like the one King Jehoash tells in 2 Kings 14:9. The doubled verb ("going they went") opens the tale with weight, much like "once upon a time". The trees stand for the lords of Shechem, and each plant for a kind of ruler.

decisions.choice: to anoint a king: to make a king by pouring oil on him
decisions.reason: Kings in Israel were made by anointing with olive oil (1 Samuel 10:1; 16:13). The trees go first to the olive, the very tree that gives the oil of anointing.

decisions.choice: Be our king
decisions.reason: "Reign over us" is said more naturally in present-day English as "Be our king"; Literal keeps "Reign over us". The same wording returns in verses 10, 12 and 14.

decisions.choice: verses 8-15 set in poetic lines
decisions.reason: The fable is set in lines, as the Hebrew accents divide it, at every level.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לָהֶם֙ הַזַּ֔יִת הֶחֳדַ֨לְתִּי֙ אֶת־דִּשְׁנִ֔י אֲשֶׁר־בִּ֛י יְכַבְּד֥וּ אֱלֹהִ֖ים וַאֲנָשִׁ֑ים וְהָ֣לַכְתִּ֔י לָנ֖וּעַ עַל־הָעֵצִֽים׃
records.gloss: And said to them the olive tree, have I ceased [from] my fatness, which by me they honor God and men, and I go to sway over the trees?
pieces: But the olive tree answered them, \q 'Should I stop giving my rich oil, \q which is used to honor God and {{gender:humans|men}}, \q and go to wave over the trees?'

L.9: But the olive tree said to them, \q 'Should I give up my richness, \q by which God and {{gender:people|men}} are honored, \q and go to sway over the trees?'

R.9: But the olive tree said, 'Should I stop making my oil, which people use to honor God and one another, \q just to wave back and forth over the trees?'

decisions.choice: my fatness: my rich oil
decisions.reason: The word means fatness or richness, here the olive's oil, the best thing it gives. Oil was used to anoint priests and kings, to honor guests, and in offerings (Leviticus 2:1; Psalm 23:5).

decisions.choice: God and men: God and human beings, all who are honored with oil
decisions.reason: The word elohim can mean God or gods. In Israel, oil and wine (verse 13) are offered to God (Leviticus 2:1; Numbers 15:5-10), and Jotham has just called on God (verse 7), so God is meant. But in a fable the pair can also be a fixed phrase, "gods and men", for everyone above and below.

decisions.choice: go to sway over the trees: give up a useful life for an empty, restless rule
decisions.reason: The verb means to wave, sway or wander (Isaiah 7:2; Psalm 109:10). Ruling is pictured as swaying back and forth above the others, with nothing produced. The good trees refuse to trade their fruitfulness for it.

decisions.choice: people / humans
decisions.reason: The word means human beings in general, as the pair "God and men" shows. Balanced and Readable use inclusive words, and the reader's gender setting can show "men".

decisions.choice: just to
decisions.reason: Readable adds "just" to bring out the scorn of the question: the trade would be a poor one.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ הָעֵצִ֖ים לַתְּאֵנָ֑ה לְכִי־אַ֖תְּ מָלְכִ֥י עָלֵֽינוּ׃
records.gloss: And said the trees to the fig tree, come you, reign over us.
pieces: Then the trees said to the fig tree, \q 'You come and be our king.'

L.10: Then the trees said to the fig tree, \q 'You come, reign over us.'

R.10: Then the trees said to the fig tree, \q 'Come and be our king.'

decisions.choice: you come, reign over us: an urgent, pressing call
decisions.reason: The added "you" presses the request on the fig tree: if the olive will not, then you. The trees go down the list of the most useful plants of the land (Deuteronomy 8:8).

records.source: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר לָהֶם֙ הַתְּאֵנָ֔ה הֶחֳדַ֨לְתִּי֙ אֶת־מָתְקִ֔י וְאֶת־תְּנוּבָתִ֖י הַטּוֹבָ֑ה וְהָ֣לַכְתִּ֔י לָנ֖וּעַ עַל־הָעֵצִֽים׃
records.gloss: And said to them the fig tree, have I ceased [from] my sweetness and my fruit, the good, and I go to sway over the trees?
pieces: But the fig tree answered them, \q 'Should I give up my sweetness and my fine fruit \q and go to wave over the trees?'

L.11: But the fig tree said to them, \q 'Should I give up my sweetness and my good fruit \q and go to sway over the trees?'

R.11: But the fig tree said, 'Should I stop making my sweet, good fruit \q just to wave back and forth over the trees?'

decisions.choice: should I give up my sweetness: the same refusal as the olive's
decisions.reason: As in verse 9. The fig would lose its sweet fruit, a staple food, to sway over the trees.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ הָעֵצִ֖ים לַגָּ֑פֶן לְכִי־אַ֖תְּ מָלְכִ֥י עָלֵֽינוּ׃
records.gloss: And said the trees to the vine, come you, reign over us.
pieces: Then the trees said to the vine, \q 'You come and be our king.'

L.12: Then the trees said to the vine, \q 'You come, reign over us.'

R.12: Then the trees said to the grapevine, \q 'Come and be our king.'

decisions.choice: you come, reign over us
decisions.reason: As in verse 10.

decisions.choice: grapevine
decisions.reason: Readable says "grapevine" to make the plant clear; Literal and Balanced keep "vine".

records.source: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר לָהֶם֙ הַגֶּ֔פֶן הֶחֳדַ֨לְתִּי֙ אֶת־תִּ֣ירוֹשִׁ֔י הַֽמְשַׂמֵּ֥חַ אֱלֹהִ֖ים וַאֲנָשִׁ֑ים וְהָ֣לַכְתִּ֔י לָנ֖וּעַ עַל־הָעֵצִֽים׃
records.gloss: And said to them the vine, have I ceased [from] my new wine, which gladdens God and men, and I go to sway over the trees?
pieces: But the vine answered them, \q 'Should I give up my new wine, \q which brings joy to God and {{gender:humans|men}}, \q and go to wave over the trees?'

L.13: But the vine said to them, \q 'Should I give up my new wine, \q which cheers God and {{gender:people|men}}, \q and go to sway over the trees?'

R.13: But the vine said, 'Should I stop making my wine, which makes God and people glad, \q just to wave back and forth over the trees?'

decisions.choice: new wine that cheers God and men: wine poured out to God and drunk at feasts
decisions.reason: Wine was poured out with the offerings as "a pleasing aroma to the LORD" (Numbers 15:7, 10) and drunk at every feast. On "God" or "gods" see verse 9. The harvest feast in Baal's temple (verse 27) gives the line a bitter echo.

decisions.choice: people / humans
decisions.reason: As in verse 9.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ כָל־הָעֵצִ֖ים אֶל־הָאָטָ֑ד לֵ֥ךְ אַתָּ֖ה מְלָךְ־עָלֵֽינוּ׃
records.gloss: And said all the trees to the bramble, come you, reign over us.
pieces: Then all the trees said to the bramble, \q 'You come and be our king.'

L.14: Then all the trees said to the bramble, \q 'You come, reign over us.'

R.14: At last all the trees said to the thornbush, \q 'Come and be our king.'

decisions.choice: the bramble: a low thorny shrub, good for nothing but burning
decisions.reason: The word names a thorny bush, probably the buckthorn of the hills of Israel (Psalm 58:10). It gives no fruit, no oil and almost no shade, and its dry wood catches fire quickly. This time "all the trees" ask, the whole city turning to the least worthy plant of all.

decisions.choice: thornbush
decisions.reason: Readable says "thornbush", a commoner word than "bramble"; it names the same plant. Readable also adds "At last", since this is the last plant the trees ask.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הָאָטָד֮ אֶל־הָעֵצִים֒ אִ֡ם בֶּאֱמֶ֣ת אַתֶּם֩ מֹשְׁחִ֨ים אֹתִ֤י לְמֶ֨לֶךְ֙ עֲלֵיכֶ֔ם בֹּ֖אוּ חֲס֣וּ בְצִלִּ֑י וְאִם־אַ֕יִן תֵּ֤צֵא אֵשׁ֙ מִן־הָ֣אָטָ֔ד וְתֹאכַ֖ל אֶת־אַרְזֵ֥י הַלְּבָנֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And said the bramble to the trees, if in truth you [are] anointing me as king over you, come, take refuge in my shade; and if not, may fire go out from the bramble and may it consume [the] cedars of Lebanon.
pieces: The bramble answered the trees, \q 'If you are truly anointing me king over you, \q come and shelter in my shade. \q Otherwise, may fire come out of the bramble \q and burn up the cedars of Lebanon!'

L.15: And the bramble said to the trees, \q 'If in truth you [are] anointing me as king over you, \q come, take refuge in my shade; \q but if not, let fire come out of the bramble \q and devour the cedars of Lebanon.'

R.15: The thornbush answered, 'If you really want me as your king, \q come and rest safely in my shade. \q But if you do not, may fire come out of the thornbush \q and burn up even the great cedar trees of Lebanon!'

decisions.choice: take refuge in my shade: trust me for protection, a promise the bramble cannot keep
decisions.reason: "Shade" is the protection a king gives his people (Isaiah 30:2-3; Lamentations 4:20). A low thornbush can give no shade to a tree; the offer is empty and the picture absurd. The bramble asks the great trees to bow down beneath it.

decisions.choice: in truth: in good faith, honestly meant
decisions.reason: The bramble asks whether the trees mean it. Jotham takes up the same words in verses 16 and 19: did the lords act "in truth" when they made Abimelech king?

decisions.choice: fire from the bramble devouring the cedars of Lebanon: the worthless ruler destroys the greatest
decisions.reason: Dry thornbushes catch fire easily and spread it to everything around them (Exodus 22:5; Isaiah 9:17). The cedars of Lebanon were the tallest and finest trees known in Israel. Jotham applies the threat in verse 20, and it comes true in verses 49 and 57.

decisions.choice: even the great cedar trees
decisions.reason: Readable adds "great" and "even" to show why the cedars are named: the fire of the smallest plant reaches the mightiest trees.

records.source: וְעַתָּ֗ה אִם־בֶּאֱמֶ֤ת וּבְתָמִים֙ עֲשִׂיתֶ֔ם וַתַּמְלִ֖יכוּ אֶת־אֲבִימֶ֑לֶךְ וְאִם־טוֹבָ֤ה עֲשִׂיתֶם֙ עִם־יְרֻבַּ֣עַל וְעִם־בֵּית֔וֹ וְאִם־כִּגְמ֥וּל יָדָ֖יו עֲשִׂ֥יתֶם לֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And now, if in truth and in integrity you have acted and made king Abimelech, and if good you have done with Jerubbaal and with his house, and if according to [the] dealing of his hands you have done to him —
pieces: So now, if you acted faithfully and honorably when you made Abimelech king, and if you have treated Jerubbaal and his family well and given him what his deeds deserved—

L.16: And now, if you have acted in truth and in integrity and made Abimelech king, and if you have done good with Jerubbaal and with his house, and if you have done to him according to the deed of his hands—

R.16: Now think about what you have done. Were you honest and right to make Abimelech king? Have you been good to Jerubbaal and his family? Have you treated him as he deserved?

decisions.choice: a broken sentence: the condition begun here is taken up again in verse 19
decisions.reason: Jotham starts a long "if ...", breaks off in verses 17-18 to remind them what Gideon did and what they have done, and then starts again in verse 19 with "if, then". The interruption is part of the speech's force.

decisions.choice: in truth and in integrity: the words of the covenant made at Shechem
decisions.reason: At Shechem Joshua told Israel to serve the LORD "in integrity and in truth" (Joshua 24:14). Jotham asks the lords of Shechem whether they have kept faith in that way with the family of the man who saved them.

decisions.choice: according to the deed of his hands: as his actions deserved
decisions.reason: "The dealing of his hands" means what a man has done for others. To do to him "according to" it is to repay him fairly for it (Proverbs 12:14; Isaiah 3:11).

decisions.choice: questions in place of the conditions
decisions.reason: Readable turns Jotham's long "if" clauses into questions, so the reader is not left waiting through verses 17-18 for the end of the sentence.

records.source: אֲשֶׁר־נִלְחַ֥ם אָבִ֖י עֲלֵיכֶ֑ם וַיַּשְׁלֵ֤ךְ אֶת־נַפְשׁוֹ֙ מִנֶּ֔גֶד וַיַּצֵּ֥ל אֶתְכֶ֖ם מִיַּ֥ד מִדְיָֽן׃
records.gloss: that fought my father for you, and threw his life from in front, and delivered you from [the] hand of Midian;
pieces: for my father fought for you, risked his life, and rescued you from the power of Midian,

L.17: for my father fought for you and threw his life away in front [of him] and delivered you from the hand of Midian;

R.17: Remember, my father fought for you. He risked his life and saved you from the Midianites.

decisions.choice: threw his life away in front of him: risked his life
decisions.reason: To "throw one's life away" is to put it in danger without holding anything back, as Jephthah says he "put his life in his hand" (12:3).

decisions.choice: delivered you from the hand of Midian: Gideon's victory in chapters 6-8
decisions.reason: For seven years Midian had stripped the land (6:1-6), until God saved Israel through Gideon (7:22; 8:28). The lords of Shechem owed their freedom to the man whose sons they have just killed.

decisions.choice: Remember
decisions.reason: Readable starts a new sentence with "Remember" for the interruption that the Hebrew joins with "for" (see verse 16).

records.gloss: and you have risen against [the] house of my father today, and killed his sons, seventy men, on one stone, and made king Abimelech, son of his female slave, over [the] lords of Shechem, for your brother [is] he —
pieces: but today you have turned against my father's family. You have killed his sons, seventy men, on a single stone, and made Abimelech, the son of his slave woman, king over the leaders of Shechem because he is your relative—

L.18: and you have risen up against the house of my father today and killed his sons, seventy men, on one stone, and made Abimelech, the son of his slave woman, king over the lords of Shechem, because he [is] your brother—

R.18: But today you have turned against my father's family. You have killed his seventy sons on one stone. Then you made Abimelech king over you, the leaders of Shechem, just because he is your relative. And he is only the son of my father's slave woman!

decisions.choice: the son of his slave woman: a mother of low, unfree standing
decisions.reason: The word amah means a female slave. In 8:31 she is called Gideon's concubine, a secondary wife. Jotham uses the lowest word he can to shame Abimelech and those who chose him: they have killed the sons of a free house for the son of a slave.

decisions.choice: you have killed his sons: you share the guilt, though Abimelech struck the blows
decisions.reason: The lords did not kill the brothers with their own hands, but they paid for it (verse 4). Jotham charges them with the murder, as the narrator does in verse 24.

decisions.choice: he is your brother: he is your kinsman
decisions.reason: Jotham throws their own words back at them (verse 3). Abimelech was also the brother of the seventy he killed.

decisions.choice: slave woman
decisions.reason: "Slave" is kept at every level, because her unfree status is the point of Jotham's insult; "servant" would lose it (see the style guide on 'eved).

decisions.choice: the insult moved to the end
decisions.reason: Readable puts the insult in a sentence of its own at the end, where it keeps its force without crowding the list of charges.
